P1_fx_receipts.question: Can resident individuals receive foreign currency for services or digital exports? Any conversion or repatriation rule?
P1_fx_receipts.answer: Yes, under exchange control (Common Monetary Area rules). The Bank of Namibia says foreign-earned income may be retained offshore, but this does not apply to export proceeds. Goods export proceeds must be repatriated within 180 days and may be held indefinitely in foreign-currency accounts at local banks. Payments for goods and services go through commercial banks (authorised dealers). Whether a freelancer's foreign client fees count as 'foreign earned income' or as service-export proceeds was not confirmed.

sources.quote: Additionally, Namibia’s exchange control law mandates that export proceeds from Namibian goods must be repatriated within 180 days from the date of shipment.

P1_fx_receipts.notes: Residents also have a N$1m single discretionary allowance and N$4m offshore investment allowance (with tax clearance) per BoN FAQ.

P2_fcy_account.question: Can resident individuals hold a foreign-currency account locally?
P2_fcy_account.answer: Yes. Export proceeds can be kept indefinitely in foreign-currency accounts at local banks and used to settle foreign liabilities. Banks offer customer foreign-currency accounts.

P2_fcy_account.notes: Individual (non-exporter) FCA eligibility not separately confirmed.

L2_tax_id.question: Tax ID: who needs one, how to get it?
L2_tax_id.answer: The TIN (Taxpayer Identification Number), issued by the Namibia Revenue Agency (NamRA) on registration. It is your official tax reference. Registration is a legal requirement for anyone liable under Namibian tax law, including individuals with business income from Namibia; registering creates a record, and tax is due only when an obligation arises (NamRA registration FAQ).

L3_income_tax_foreign.question: Income tax on foreign-source income for residents; rates or special regimes
L3_income_tax_foreign.answer: Namibia taxes on a source basis: individuals are taxable on income received or accrued from a Namibian or deemed Namibian source (Deloitte 2026; PwC). Rates for the year from 1 March 2025: 0% up to NAD 100,000, then 18% rising in bands to 37% above NAD 1,550,000 (PwC; Deloitte 2026). Whether fees for remote work done in Namibia for foreign clients are Namibian-source (likely, since the work is performed there) was not confirmed. The 2026/27 budget proposed new brackets that were not yet enacted when checked (search summary).

L4_vat_gst.question: VAT/GST: rate, registration threshold, treatment of exported digital services
L4_vat_gst.answer: VAT is 15%. Registration became mandatory above N$1,000,000 of taxable supplies in any 12 months, doubled from N$500,000 under recent amendments. The planned April 2026 e-invoicing launch was turned into a phased multi-year rollout. Treatment of exported services was not established.

L6_consumer_ecommerce.question: Consumer-protection / e-commerce rules for online sales (refunds, disclosures)
L6_consumer_ecommerce.answer: The Electronic Transactions Act 4 of 2019 contains a consumer chapter: a 7-day cooling-off right (s. 35), and cancellation within 14 days if the supplier fails its information duties. Per the annotated statute, that chapter (Chapter 4) is NOT yet in force, so these rights cannot currently be relied on. General consumer law applies meanwhile.

W1_workarounds.question: Simple, legal routes around payment barriers for a beginner (no misrepresentation, nominees or sanctions evasion)
W1_workarounds.answer: Barriers: Stripe does not accept merchants here; platforms that pay out through PayPal Payouts cannot pay PayPal accounts here (not on PayPal's Payouts list, see P4 for ordinary PayPal receiving); Wise does not let residents hold money. Simple legal routes: (1) Sell digital products or software through a merchant of record: Paddle (software/SaaS only; each seller reviewed), Lemon Squeezy (bank payouts), Polar, Dodo Payments. The platform is the legal seller to your customers, handles card payments and consumer VAT/sales tax, and pays you out. You still declare the payouts as your income at home (see L3). (2) Sell services on Upwork, which is available here (not on its restricted list). Which withdrawal methods you get (bank, PayPal, Payoneer, etc.) depends on the country and shows in your account. (3) Paid apps and in-app sales through Google Play (merchant registration available here). (4) For direct clients, a bank transfer (SWIFT) into your own local account always works. Follow the local foreign-exchange rules (see P1) and keep invoices. Avoid: opening accounts with a foreign address, a relative's or friend's identity, or a VPN to look like you are elsewhere. It breaches platform terms (accounts and funds get frozen) and can break anti-money-laundering or sanctions law.
